summary: The speakers (Yuval Belfer and Niv Granot from AI21 Labs) argue that RAG evaluation is fundamentally flawed. Most benchmarks consist of local questions with local answers, assuming answers lie in specific document chunks. Even multi-hop benchmarks like Google's Frames use manufactured, unrealistic questions. Benchmarks are typically either retrieval-only or generation-only, failing to test systems holistically — missing chunking, parsing, and cases where answers don't map to specific locations. This creates a vicious cycle: developers optimize for flawed benchmarks, celebrate high scores publicly, but users struggle on real data. The cycle repeats with new benchmarks carrying the same problems. The speakers highlight aggregative questions as a key failure mode. Financial data questions like which company reported the highest quarterly revenue most times require counting, max/min, and calculation across documents. Standard RAG pipelines that retrieve top-k chunks cannot answer these because there is always an n+1 chunk that might contain relevant data. They demonstrate this with a 22-document FIFA World Cup corpus from Wikipedia. Common RAG pipelines (LangChain, LlamaIndex) achieve only 5% and 11% accuracy on questions like which team has won the World Cup the most times. Their proposed solution — structured RAG — converts unstructured corpora into relational data structures. During ingestion, documents are clustered into subcorpuses, schemas are identified per corpus, schemas are populated per document, and results are uploaded to an SQL database. At inference, the system identifies the relevant schema and performs text-to-SQL. They acknowledge significant limitations: not every corpus is relational or homogeneous, normalization is challenging (West Germany vs. Germany, singular vs. list attributes), ambiguity exists, LLMs tend to please users, and text-to-SQL becomes complex with large schemas. The main takeaway is that RAG is not one-size-fits-all; the standard chunking-embedding-retrieving-reranking pipeline is insufficient for many real-world use cases.

sections.title: Introduction and the Problem with RAG Benchmarks
sections.summary: Speakers introduce themselves as Yuval and Niv from AI21 Labs. They argue RAG evaluation is broken because benchmarks use local questions with local answers, assuming answers reside in specific chunks. Multi-hop benchmarks like Google's Frames use unrealistic manufactured questions. Benchmarks are either retrieval-only or generation-only, missing holistic system testing including chunking and parsing. A vicious cycle exists: developers optimize for flawed benchmarks, celebrate high scores, but users struggle on real data.

sections.title: Aggregative Questions and Top-k Retrieval Failure
sections.summary: The speakers explain that financial data questions (e.g., FinanceBench, SEC filings) often require aggregative answers: counting, max/min, or calculation across documents. Standard RAG pipelines that grab top-k chunks cannot handle these because there is always an n+1 chunk that might contain relevant data. Questions like 'which company reported the highest quarterly revenue most times' or 'in how many fiscal years did Apple exceed 100 billion' expose this limitation.

sections.title: FIFA World Cup Corpus Experiment
sections.summary: The speakers built a 22-document corpus from FIFA World Cup Wikipedia pages and asked aggregative questions like which team won the most times or how many World Cups Brazil participated in. Common RAG pipelines (LangChain, LlamaIndex with open responses) failed with only 5% and 11% accuracy respectively, despite answers being findable in local segments.

sections.title: Structured RAG Solution
sections.summary: The proposed solution converts unstructured corpora into SQL data structures. During ingestion: documents are clustered into subcorpuses (e.g., financial vs. FIFA), schemas are identified per corpus (year, winner, top three teams, top scorer), schemas are populated per document using an LLM pipeline, and results are uploaded to an SQL database. At inference: the relevant schema is identified for the query and text-to-SQL retrieves the answer.

sections.title: Limitations and Main Takeaways
sections.summary: The approach has limitations: not every corpus is relational or homogeneous, normalization is difficult (West Germany vs. Germany, singular vs. list host country), ambiguity exists (Real Madrid in World Cup context), LLMs try to please users, and text-to-SQL is complex with large schemas. Main takeaways: RAG is not one-size-fits-all, standard chunking-embedding-retrieving-reranking is insufficient for many questions, existing benchmarks fail to capture these use cases, and solutions may need to go beyond standard RAG for specific settings.
